text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, vaccination is an important part of disease prevention, but it works alongside — not instead of — good nutrition, clean water, suitable housing, hygiene, biosecurity, disease monitoring, and responsible animal movement. The appropriate vaccination program depends on species, age, production purpose, vaccination history, local disease presence, and guidance from Cambodian veterinary/animal-health services — cattle, pigs, and poultry require different strategies, and a chicken schedule should never be applied to ducks. During the wet season (roughly May–October), muddy conditions and contaminated equipment can complicate hygiene; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat, dust, and maintaining vaccine storage conditions become concerns. Vaccines are biological products that can lose effectiveness outside the manufacturer's required temperature range — smallholders with limited refrigeration should coordinate vaccination with a veterinarian, animal-health worker, or cooperative rather than storing vaccines indefinitely at home. Keep a simple vaccination record (animal/flock, vaccine name, date, batch if available). Exact vaccine dose, dilution, route, age, timing, and booster interval must never be inferred by the AI — these must come from a veterinarian, competent animal-health professional, or the current registered product label. No specific Cambodian vaccination calendar or predominant breed is asserted here due to insufficient current province-specific evidence.
